extracted.intended_audience: learned readers: natural philosophers, experimentalists, and theological readers of early-modern natural theology
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative natural-philosophy treatise using observational experiments and natural-law reasoning to prove Divine Providence, explain fertility (saltpetre/air) and to answer objections to the possibility of resurrection. Mixes experimental reports with philosophical/theological inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and symmetry of the world as evidence of a Creator
rubrics_metrics.description: The great and amazing Machine the World, with order and symmetry, where parts render services to one another and particles assume figure or motion according to certain laws, is evidence of a Creator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: from observed regularity, mutual subordination of parts, and lawful behaviour of particles (e.g. bodies cannot assume motion or figure except according to prescribed laws), one infers design. Examples: coordination among parts of the world; uniform behaviours such as juice of the grape producing wine 'so uniformly and constantly'. Anti-pattern: explaining order as arising from a mere confused heap of particles without laws or wisdom is deemed incredible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation/continuation of things as proof of God
rubrics_metrics.description: The preserving and continuing of all things in the state and condition in which they were first created provides evidence for God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: beyond the original laws producing things, the ongoing maintenance (preservation) of those things in their proper ordered states implies an intelligent Director. Use as a standard when arguing that mere chance or material motion cannot account for sustained order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex organized bodies cannot arise from chaotic particles without laws
rubrics_metrics.description: From a confused heap of particles (air, earth, water, fire) it is incredible that so many determinate small stamina (seeds) and glorious machines (bodies of men, beasts, plants) should arise frequently and uniformly without governing laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses thought-experiments (imagine particles at rest, mixture of vapours, effluvia) and observations (fermentation smells, rusting of iron, perfumes travelling leagues) to argue that chance cannot reliably produce consistent, complex organisms. Anti-pattern: positing random motions of particles to explain reproducible biological structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawfulness required to explain species-fidelity in seeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Each seed always produces its own plant of the same kind and virtue every year without failing, which indicates that certain laws operate to cause only proper particles to unite with each seed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative test: sowing different seeds together in same earth, water, and air still yields each seed producing its characteristic plant — explained by laws that cause particles necessary to each seed to unite only with that seed. The page criticizes chance-based accounts (e.g., pores admitting random particles) as inadequate (Pitcairn's mathematical objection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of mechanical 'pores in seeds' hypothesis as insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis that seeds have pores or orifices admitting only appropriately sized particles, allowing chance or necessity (without direction) to produce growth, is inadequate to explain consistent development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and example: throwing a dye through a square hole — to get the same result repeatedly requires repetition and a rule; mathematically, mere chance would rarely supply the exact same particles in the same order. Thus a rule or law (or divine direction) must be posited. Use as a standard to reject purely mechanical random-admission explanations for reproducible biological form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seed contains miniature form (stamen) implying direction
rubrics_metrics.description: All known seeds are formed of an exceedingly small stamen containing the parts in miniature, from which expansion/unfolding and accretion of matter produce full organisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical support: microscopic observations. Inferential use: the presence of such minute pre-formed structure makes accidental concourse of particles implausible as the cause; thus law or directed providence is invoked. Use this as evidence when evaluating causal accounts of development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of systematic experiments to detect nitre (salt-petre) in the air (Seven experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of seven experiments and observations are offered to show that either saltpetre, or something nitrous, exists in the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments enumerated/described on the page: I) Earth mixed with filings of iron, urine, dung, etc., exposed to air yields salt-petre; II) Blood turned red by contact with air and nitre; III) Salt-petre can be made from blood (suggesting air leaves nitrous quality in blood); IV) refined salt-petre emits air-bubbles when put in Lye and placed in an air-pump, suggesting air in salt-petre; V) salt-petre held in burning-glasses evaporates to mingle with air; VI) metals corroding in air (rust) suggests nitrous-like matter in air (gold excepted); VII) closed rooms with many people and stoves cause faintness that is alleviated by nitrous salts, suggesting nitrous parts are involved in respiration/fire. Guidance: these empirical signs are presented collectively as grounds to infer aerial nitre; they serve as standards for concluding presence of nitrous matter in air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical origin of aerial nitre: northward source evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical indications (three points) suggest that the aerial nitre or nitrous matter comes chiefly from the North (northerly winds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support cited: I) cold northern air and ice mountains suggesting nitre abundance; II) observations that exudation of nitre from mortar/walls appears most in winter and with northerly winds and more on north-facing walls; III) barometric/thermometric arguments (northerly winds making air heavier). Use these as criteria to infer source-directionality of atmospheric constituents affecting fertility and climate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salt-petre becomes active by conjunction with sulphureous particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Salt-petre alone is relatively inactive; when combined with sulphureous bodies (sulphur, antimony, turf, charcoal, tartar—the 'sulphureous' class) it becomes active, producing flame and motion (e.g., gunpowder), showing how nitrous and sulphureous aerial matters interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments and examples: mixing salt-petre with sulphur, charcoal or tartar produces violent motion and flame; tartar + salt-petre burns and leaves an alkaline fixed salt; gunpowder cited as striking instance. Use this chemical interaction as explanatory mechanism for observed thunderstorms, lightning, and activity in the atmosphere when nitre and sulphur co-occur. Also notes rays of the sun can volatilize salt-petre, aiding interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salt-petre and solar rays contribute to soil fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: Salt-petre (nitre) in conjunction with the rays of the sun (or solar matter) contributes to the fertility of the earth and to plant growth; seeds steeped in salt-petre water grow more fruitfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical examples: steeping seeds in water with dissolved salt-petre produced plants a third higher; experiment with purslain and French-beans in 1711/1712; observation that northerly winds followed by warm southern sun often produce early good crops. Also notes extreme amounts can be detrimental (too much salt-petre can kill plants). Use these observations as experimental criteria when assessing causes of fertility and proposing agricultural treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate continued experimental inquiry and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Encouragement to further experiments to examine what renders lands fertile, to verify or falsify hypotheses about aerial nitre, solar matter, and seed treatment; notes many experiments remain wanting and calls for detailed trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested practical experiments: ordering earths or seeds to produce a salad in hours, inducing all seed-plants in a seed to grow equally, reproducing salt-petre fertility effects under varied conditions. Standard: prioritize clear circumstances, reproducibility, and communication of results to the world. Use as a methodological rubric for natural-philosophical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument that objections to resurrection are not stronger than God's power
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical-theological criterion: objections to the possibility of bodily resurrection (e.g., Sadducees' ridicule) are answered by scriptural authority and by noting that creating a body is no greater miracle than raising it; the few known laws of nature do not render resurrection impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: appeal to Matt. xxii.29 ('you do err, not knowing the Scriptures, nor the Power of God') and the comparative claim that raising a body is not a greater miracle than creating one. Use this as standard when evaluating philosophical objections: compare alleged impossibility to divine omnipotence and to the limits of current natural-law understanding.
